claims.text: The as-synthesized high-entropy alloy has a nearly random atomic distribution.
The as-synthesized alloy has no observable superconductivity at low temperature.
Changing the cooling rate below approximately 10 K can permit or inhibit formation of local short-range atomic order.
Slow cooling permits more short-range atomic order than rapid quenching.
Emergent short-range atomic order modifies localized phonon modes.
Short-range atomic order enhances local electron–phonon interactions.
Disorder-related scattering suppresses superconductivity in the alloy.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling can overcome disorder-related scattering.
Overcoming disorder-related scattering promotes Cooper-pair formation at sufficiently low temperature.
Slowly cooled samples will exhibit a superconducting transition below a characteristic temperature.
The predicted superconducting state will be evidenced by zero electrical resistance.
The predicted superconducting state will exhibit a measurable Meissner effect.
Rapidly quenched samples will exhibit little or no superconductivity under otherwise identical test conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies only when cooling is sufficiently slow to permit atomic reordering.
Cooling faster than an unspecified threshold may prevent the superconducting effect.
Impurities or mechanical stress may dominate the response and prevent the proposed effect from being observed.

contradictions.description: The intervention attributes ordering to cooling-rate differences within the regime below approximately 10 K, whereas the falsification design proposes slow cooling from a high temperature. These are materially different thermal histories, so the temperature interval in which ordering is hypothesized to form is inconsistent.
